content: 1. NovoLog has not been studied in pediatric patients younger than 2 years of age. 2. NovoLog has not been evaluated in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes. 3. In three controlled clinical studies involving 1,375 patients treated with NovoLog, 2.6% (36 patients) were aged 65 years or older. 4. Among these elderly patients, half had type 1 diabetes (18 out of 1,285), and the other half had type 2 diabetes (18 out of 90). 5. The HbA1c response to NovoLog, compared to human insulin, did not differ by age, particularly in patients with type 2 diabetes. 6. Additional studies in larger populations of patients aged 65 years or older are needed to draw conclusions about the safety of NovoLog in elderly patients compared to younger patients. 7. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to assess the effect of age on the onset of NovoLog action have not been conducted. 8. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart (NovoLog) with respect to specific gender populations. 9. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart in specific racial populations. 10. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart in patients with renal impairment. 11. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart in patients with hepatic impairment. 12. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart in women of reproductive potential or in males. 13. There is no FDA guidance on the use of insulin aspart in immunocompromised patients. 14. NovoLog can be administered via intravenous or subcutaneous routes. 15. Careful glucose monitoring and dose adjustments of insulin, including NovoLog, may be necessary in patients with renal dysfunction. 16. Careful glucose monitoring and dose adjustments of insulin, including NovoLog, may be necessary in patients with hepatic dysfunction. 17. Limited information is available regarding the intravenous compatibility of insulin aspart in the drug label. 18. Acute overdose of insulin, particularly when administered intravenously, may cause hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. 19. Mild episodes of hypoglycemia can usually be treated with oral glucose. 20. Adjustments in drug dosage, meal patterns, or exercise may be required to manage hypoglycemia. 21. Severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure, or neurologic impairment may require treatment with intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon or concentrated intravenous glucose. 22. Sustained carbohydrate intake and observation may be necessary because hypoglycemia can recur after apparent clinical recovery. 23. Hypokalemia must be corrected appropriately. 24. Limited information is available regarding chronic overdose of insulin aspart in the drug label. 25. The primary activity of NovoLog is the regulation of glucose metabolism. 26. Insulins, including NovoLog, bind to insulin receptors on muscle and fat cells, lowering blood glucose by facilitating cellular glucose uptake and inhibiting hepatic glucose output. 27. NovoLog is a rapid-acting human insulin analog used to lower blood glucose. 28. NovoLog is homologous to regular human insulin, except for a single substitution of proline with aspartic acid at position B28, and is produced using recombinant DNA technology in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast). 29. Insulin aspart has the empirical formula C256H381N65O79S6 and a molecular weight of 5,825. 30. NovoLog is a sterile, aqueous, clear, and colorless solution containing insulin aspart 100 Units/mL, glycerin 16 mg/mL, phenol 1.50 mg/mL, metacresol 1.72 mg/mL, zinc 19.6 mcg/mL, disodium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate 1.25 mg/mL, sodium chloride 0.58 mg/mL, and water for injection. 31. NovoLog has a pH of 7.2–7.6, which may be adjusted with hydrochloric acid 10% and/or sodium hydroxide 10%. 32. Studies in normal volunteers and patients with diabetes demonstrated that subcutaneous administration of NovoLog has a more rapid onset of action than regular human insulin. 33. In a study of patients with type 1 diabetes, the maximum glucose-lowering effect of NovoLog occurred between 1 and 3 hours after subcutaneous injection. 34. The duration of action for NovoLog is 3 to 5 hours. 35. The time course of action of insulin and insulin analogs, such as NovoLog, may vary significantly between individuals or within the same individual. 36. The parameters of NovoLog activity (onset time, peak time, and duration) should be considered as general guidelines. 37. The rate of insulin absorption and onset of activity is influenced by the injection site, exercise, and other variables. 38. A double-blind, randomized, two-way crossover study in 16 patients with type 1 diabetes demonstrated that intravenous infusion of NovoLog resulted in a blood glucose profile similar to that of regular human insulin. 39. NovoLog or human insulin was infused until the patient’s blood glucose decreased to 36 mg/dL or until signs of hypoglycemia (e.g., increased heart rate and sweating) were observed, defined as the time of autonomic reaction. 40. The substitution of proline with aspartic acid at position B28 in NovoLog reduces the molecule's tendency to form hexamers, as observed with regular human insulin. 41. NovoLog is absorbed more rapidly after subcutaneous injection compared to regular human insulin. 42. In a randomized, double-blind, crossover study, 17 healthy Caucasian male subjects aged 18 to 40 years received an intravenous infusion of either NovoLog or regular human insulin at 1.5 mU/kg/min for 120 minutes. 43. The mean insulin clearance was similar for the two groups, with mean values of 1.2 L/h/kg for both NovoLog and regular human insulin. 44. NovoLog has faster absorption, a faster onset of action, and a shorter duration of action than regular human insulin after subcutaneous injection. 45. The relative bioavailability of NovoLog compared to regular human insulin indicates that the two insulins are absorbed to a similar extent. 46. In studies involving healthy volunteers and patients with type 1 diabetes, NovoLog consistently reached peak serum concentrations approximately twice as fast as regular human insulin. 47. The median time to maximum concentration in these trials was 40 to 50 minutes for NovoLog versus 80 to 120 minutes for regular human insulin. 48. In a clinical trial in patients with type 1 diabetes, NovoLog and regular human insulin, both administered subcutaneously at a dose of 0.15 U/kg body weight, reached mean maximum concentrations of 82 and 36 mU/L, respectively. 49. The pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic characteristics of insulin aspart have not been established in patients with type 2 diabetes. 50. The intra-individual variability in time to maximum serum insulin concentration for healthy male volunteers was significantly less for NovoLog than for regular human insulin. 51. The clinical significance of this observation has not been established. 52. In a clinical study in healthy non-obese subjects, the pharmacokinetic differences between NovoLog and regular human insulin were observed regardless of the injection site (abdomen, thigh, or upper arm).
